situations.title: Travel in China
situations.intro: Getting around mainland China: greetings, help, transport, hotels, food, paying and emergencies.

scenes.title: Greetings and politeness basics
scenes.description: What a traveller says all day: hello to one person, to a group and politely; thank you and the replies; sorry vs excuse me (对不起 / 不好意思 / 打扰一下 / 请问); goodbye; short yes/no-type answers; declining an offer; plus the formulas shop and restaurant staff say to you.

phrases.english: Hello! / Hi!
phrases.usage: The all-purpose greeting to one person (HSK level 1). Official listening items use it as a greeting (女：你好！ 男：你好！很高兴认识你。) and, very usefully for travellers, as the polite attention-getter before a request to shop staff, a cashier or a taxi driver: 你好，这个电视多少钱？ / 你好，鱼怎么卖呢？ / 你好，我去世界公园。 / 你好，一共多少钱？ You will hear 你好 or 您好 back. For older people or formal situations use 您好 (see below). With friends, family and people you see every day 你好 sounds stiff — greet them by name or title, with 早 in the morning, or casually (see the rule on greeting people you know).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: Thank you! / Thanks!
phrases.usage: Standard thanks (HSK level 1). Add a pronoun for warmth or respect: 谢谢你 / 谢谢您 (polite) / 谢谢你们 (to several people). The usual reply you will hear is 不客气. The second syllable is neutral tone in the dictionary form (xièxie).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: You're welcome.
phrases.usage: The standard reply to 谢谢 (HSK level 1): 男：谢谢你们！ 女：不客气。再见。 / 男：谢谢！麻烦你们了。 女：不客气。 Dictionary alternatives with the same job: 别客气 'don't mention it; no formalities, please', 不用谢 'You're welcome', 应该的 '(polite response) you're welcome; just doing my duty' (all CC-CEDICT). Pronunciation: 不 is bù in citation form but is said bú before the fourth tone of 客 — that is why the HSK syllabus prints 'bú kèqi'.
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: I'm sorry.
phrases.usage: A real apology when you did something wrong or caused trouble. 现汉: '对人有愧，常用为表示抱歉的套语' (feeling one has wronged someone; the usual formula of apology), e.g. 对不起，让您久等了 'sorry to keep you waiting'. The normal reply is 没关系 (paired exactly so in the HSK 3.0 level-1 sample). Staff also use it when refusing: 先生，对不起，我们这儿不能抽烟。 For small everyday slips 不好意思 is the lighter choice (see rule).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: That's OK. / It doesn't matter.
phrases.usage: The reply to 对不起 or 不好意思. Also accepts a small problem: 男：好吧，没关系。 (after hearing no window seat is left). 没事 / 没事儿 is also heard in reassurance: 没事，不用担心 'it's nothing, don't worry'.

phrases.english: Sorry. / Excuse me. (for a small inconvenience)
phrases.usage: Light apology for small slips or for troubling someone: 甲：你的词典呢？ 乙：不好意思，我没拿来。 / 不好意思，我忘记拿词典了，下星期一还你行吗？ / 真不好意思，初次见面我就迟到了，让你久等了。 It is also the everyday “excuse me” before a request (不好意思，我迷路了。 “Excuse me, I’m lost.”), and staff use it when they can’t help (不好意思，这里不能地铁直达。 “Sorry, the metro doesn’t go there directly.”). In native-speaker service dialogues it is about four times as frequent as 对不起. CC-CEDICT lists “to be sorry (for inconveniencing sb)” next to “to feel embarrassed” (the 5th-edition 现汉 text available here gives only the “embarrassed / too shy to” senses). HSK 2025: level 2.
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: Excuse me. (sorry to bother you)
phrases.usage: Say it to approach a stranger or interrupt someone; in the official examples it is followed by 请问 and the question: 打扰一下，请问，地铁站离这儿远吗？ / 打扰一下，请问在哪儿买票？ The current HSK 3.0 level-4 sample uses it to interrupt students: 打扰一下，同学，请不要在自习室里大声讨论。 When you leave after taking someone's time you can say 打扰了 ('sorry to have bothered you', CC-CEDICT), as in 好的，那我过一会儿再联系吧，打扰了，再见。
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Excuse me, what time is it?
phrases.usage: 请问 'may I ask' is the polite opener for any question to a stranger (现汉: 敬辞，用于请求对方回答问题; CC-CEDICT: 'Excuse me, may I ask...?'). Put it right before the question: 请问，这个电视多少钱？ / 请问洗手间在哪儿？ It can follow 你好/您好 or 打扰一下. This exact question is the example item of both the HSK 3.0 level-1 sample paper and the 2025 new-HSK samples.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Hello! (polite)
phrases.usage: Polite hello with the respectful 'you' 您 (现汉: 你/你们 '含敬意', with respect). In official dialogues it is what service staff say to customers (您好，请问您去哪儿？ — taxi driver; 先生，您好，您要办理什么业务？ — bank clerk; 您好！欢迎光临。 — restaurant). Use it yourself with older people, in formal settings, or to be extra polite before a favour: 您好！您能帮我们照张相吗？
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: 您 is routine in Beijing and the north; many southern speakers, whose home dialects have no 你/您 distinction, use it less among themselves (forum reports, anecdotal). 您好 from service staff is normal everywhere, and using 您 to older people — for example a partner’s parents — is polite in any region.

phrases.english: No thanks. (no need)
phrases.usage: Polite refusal of an offer: 女：吃点儿蛋糕吧？很好吃。 男：不用了，谢谢。 Add a reason to soften it: 不用了，我自己打车就行，谢谢你。 (“No need — I’ll just take a taxi, thank you”) / 不用了，谢谢您，我自己能行。 现汉: 不用 = “表示事实上没有必要” (there is no need). It is also the friendly way to wave off a street seller or tout; if someone keeps pushing, the firmer 不要，谢谢 (next phrase) is normal. To a shop assistant who comes over you can say 我只是看看 (“I’m just looking”).
phrases.speaker: me

rules.rule: The level-1 politeness core is 你好 / 谢谢 / 对不起 / 再见, with the replies 不客气 (to thanks) and 没关系 (to an apology). Learners are expected to recognise and exchange these in meeting, parting and everyday situations.
rules.why: The 2025 HSK task syllabus (in force 2026-07) lists exchanging exactly these as a level-1 communicative task; the HSK 3.0 level-1 sample tests the 对不起 → 没关系 and 谢谢 → 不客气 pairs.

rules.rule: 您 is the respectful 'you'. Service staff address customers with 您 / 您好 (您好，请问您去哪儿？ / 您稍等). Use 您 yourself with older people, people you want to show respect to, and in formal situations. In the official dialogues customers address shop staff, clerks and drivers with 你好 + their request (你好，这个电视多少钱？ / 你好，鱼怎么卖呢？ / 你好，我想办一张信用卡。 / 你好，一共多少钱？).
rules.why: 现汉 defines 您 as 你/你们 with respect ('含敬意'); the official HSK dialogues consistently show staff using 您 and customers opening with 你好.
rules.regional_note: Forum reports (anecdotal) say 您 is used routinely in Beijing, even between colleagues, while many southern speakers — whose home dialects, such as Shanghainese, have no 你/您 distinction — use it less in everyday Mandarin. Service staff say 您 everywhere, and 您 to older people (for example a partner’s parents) is polite in any region.

rules.rule: Addressing people you don't know: get staff's attention with 你好 or, in restaurants and hotels, 服务员 (服务员，请给我来一杯咖啡。 / 服务员，我们想再要一个菜。). Call a taxi driver or any skilled worker (a cook 厨师傅, a carpenter 木匠师傅) 师傅 (师傅，我去火车站。); 师傅 also follows a surname (王师傅). Staff will call you 先生 'sir' or 女士 'madam' (both HSK level 1). Students are addressed as 同学 (同学，请问图书馆怎么走？ / 打扰一下，同学，……).
rules.why: 现汉: 师傅 = '对有技艺的人的尊称' (respectful title for someone with a skill/trade), 服务员 = staff who serve guests in hotels, restaurants etc.; CC-CEDICT adds 'respectful form of address for older men' for 师傅. The forms are shown in use in official HSK/YCT dialogues.

rules.rule: In mainland China do not call a waitress or shop assistant 小姐 on its own: the word picked up the slang sense “sex worker”, and the older textbooks that taught it are out of date. Use 服务员 or 你好 instead (美女 / 帅哥 in casual places — see the next rule). Surname + 小姐 (王小姐 “Ms Wang”) is still fine in formal and business settings, and 女士 is the safe formal “madam”. In Taiwan and Hong Kong 小姐 for staff is still normal.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT records the slang sense “(slang) prostitute” for 小姐. The 2009-2010 Hanban HSK papers still had customers call female staff 小姐 (小姐，请问表演什么时候开始？ / 小姐，你好，你这儿有杯子吗？); the national 2021 standard listed 小姐 at level 1, but the 2025 HSK syllabus moved it to level 5, and none of the HSK 3.0 / 2025 sample items examined uses it as a call to staff. Current teaching sources (Kaiwa 2026, italki, Digmandarin, Chinese-forums) agree that bare 小姐 is avoided for staff in the mainland while 王小姐-style name + 小姐 remains usable.
rules.regional_note: Teaching sources say the negative connotation is felt most strongly in northern cities such as Beijing and Harbin and less in the south — but avoiding bare 小姐 for staff is the safe choice everywhere in the mainland.

rules.rule: 美女 (“beautiful woman”) and 帅哥 (“handsome guy”) are widely used as casual forms of address, especially to call young staff in shops and restaurants. They are informal, and some people find them a bit tacky (土) or uncomfortable, so with older people or in formal places stick to 你好, 服务员, 师傅 and 先生 / 女士.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT lists “handsome (form of address)” under 帅哥; the dictionaries do not record the address use of 美女, but magazine and teaching sources do: The World of Chinese (2018) says both are still used in the service industry (popular from the mid-2000s to the early 2010s, with a somewhat working-class flavour); Digmandarin calls them relaxed address terms between peers; a Kunming forum thread reports 美女 / 帅哥 as the local way to call waiting staff, with some finding it “uncouth” and younger educated speakers preferring 服务员; a 2026 teaching blog recommends 美女 for staff only in casual places.

rules.rule: Choose the “sorry / excuse me” word by situation: 对不起 = apology when you have wronged or troubled someone (reply 没关系); 不好意思 = lighter “sorry” for small slips and inconveniences, and the everyday “excuse me” before a request; 抱歉 = “sorry”, used e.g. by staff and in announcements (抱歉，先生，这里禁止吸烟。 / 我们很抱歉地通知您……); 打扰一下 = “excuse me” when approaching or interrupting someone; 请问 = “may I ask”, placed directly before a question. Sequence attested for approaching strangers: 打扰一下，请问，… ？ In Beijing you may also hear 劳驾 (“excuse me / may I trouble you”, also to get past people); it is northern and rather old-fashioned, so use 请问, 不好意思 or 打扰一下 yourself — especially in the south.
rules.why: 现汉 defines 对不起 as the apology formula for having wronged someone and 请问 as an honorific for asking someone to answer a question; CC-CEDICT gives 不好意思 “to be sorry (for inconveniencing sb)” and 打扰了 “sorry to interrupt you”; the official dialogues show each word in these roles. On 劳驾: teaching and dictionary sites (HanyuGuide, FluentU, That’s Mandarin) describe it as northern and old-fashioned, the 2025 HSK syllabus places it at levels 7-9, and native-speaker dialogue corpora use 请问 about 700 times as often.

rules.rule: Spoken morning greeting: 早 or 早上好. 早安 also means “good morning”, but in the mainland it is mostly written (good-morning messages on WeChat and social media) and more usual in Taiwan; said aloud it can sound a little formal or literary. 晚安 means “good night” when parting, not “good evening” as a greeting (that is 晚上好).
rules.why: 现汉 entries 早 (sense ❺), 早安 (“多见于翻译作品” in the 5th-edition text) and 晚安 (“用于晚上道别”); CC-CEDICT 晚上好 “Good evening!”; the 新华 词语 data defines 早安 as a greeting formula (“套语。用于早晨见面时互相问候”); teaching sites (Migaku, Preply) describe 早上好 as the mainland standard and 早安 as typical of Taiwan and written messages.

rules.rule: 你好 is for strangers, service staff and first meetings. With friends, family and people you see every day it sounds stiff and formal. Greet them instead by name or title (老师好 to a teacher), with 早 in the morning, with a casual 嗨 / 哈喽 (common among younger people), with a small question about their day (吃了吗？ “have you eaten?”, 去哪儿？ “where are you off to?”), or with 好久不见 when you haven’t met for a while.
rules.why: Teaching sites (LTL, Hack Chinese, New Concept Mandarin, an Everyday Chinese course) describe 你好 as formal, used mainly when meeting someone new and not normally among friends, and list these alternatives; native-speaker dialogue writers open casually with 哈喽 / 嗨 as well as 你好.

scenes.title: When you don't understand
scenes.description: Signalling that you didn't hear or didn't understand, asking for a repeat, checking meaning and pronunciation, saying how much Chinese you speak, asking for English, and asking someone to wait.

phrases.english: I didn't understand (what you said).
phrases.usage: Say it when you heard the words but didn't understand them: 男：天“短”了是什么意思？我没听懂。 / 女：对不起，我没听懂，您说得太快了。 没听懂 = didn't catch/understand this time. For a general inability (e.g. a strong accent or dialect) the dictionary form is 听不懂 'unable to make sense of what one is hearing' (CC-CEDICT), as in the national standard's example 刚来中国时，他一句中文也听不懂。
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.pinyin: Nǐ shuō shénme? Wǒ méi tīngjiàn.
phrases.literal: you say what? I not hear-perceive
phrases.english: What did you say? I didn't hear (you).
phrases.usage: For when you literally didn’t hear (noise, a bad phone line). 没听见 = didn’t hear; 没听懂 = heard but didn’t understand. On the phone: 女：喂？你听见我说话了吗？ 男：你说什么？你再说一次？ With a stranger a softer opener is 不好意思，我没听清楚 (“sorry, I didn’t catch that”) — 现汉’s example: 你刚才说的话我没听清楚，你从起头儿再说一遍。
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.usage: SLOT CHANGED: the source sentence is 你会说汉语吗？ ('Do you speak Chinese?'); only the language name was replaced (汉语 → 英语). 英文 is also used for 'English' (CC-CEDICT gives both 英语 and 英文 as 'English (language)'; national standard example: 除了英文，他还会说中文。). phrases.english: I've only learned a little Chinese.
phrases.usage: Shortened from the national standard's example 在来中国以前，我只学过一点儿中文。 ('Before coming to China I had only studied a little Chinese'): the time phrase 在来中国以前 was dropped (time slot); keep it if it fits. phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 一点儿 with the -r ending is northern (Beijing) speech; speakers from the south usually say 一点 (yīdiǎn): 我只学过一点中文。

rules.rule: Pick the verb for what went wrong: 没听见 = I didn’t hear it; 没听懂 = I heard it but didn’t understand; 听不懂 = I can’t understand (the speech/language — also a dialect: 我听不懂粤语 “I can’t understand Cantonese”); 看不懂 = I can’t make sense of something written or seen (sign, map, menu); 不明白 = I don’t understand the meaning or the point.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT: 听见 'to hear', 听懂 'to understand (on hearing)', 听不懂 'unable to make sense of what one is hearing', 看不懂 'unable to make sense of what one is looking at'; 现汉 明白 ❹ '知道；了解'. Official items use them exactly so (你说什么？我没听见。 / 我没听懂 / 这张地图我看不懂 / 有个句子的意思我不明白).

scenes.title: Asking for help and directions
scenes.description: Asking where something is and how to get there, whether it is far, finding the toilet or a metro station, saying you are lost, asking a stranger for a favour — and the typical answers you will hear (go straight, turn left/right, opposite, right ahead, not far).

phrases.english: Excuse me, where is the toilet?
phrases.usage: Pattern 请问 + place + 在哪儿？ Official exchange: 男：请问洗手间在哪儿？ 女：您向前走，左边就是。 Also attested with 哪里: 请问，男洗手间在哪里？ ('Where is the men's toilet?'). 洗手间 is the polite word (现汉: 婉辞，指厕所). Swap the place (slot): 地铁站 metro station, 出口 exit, 二零四房间 room 204 (请问，二零四房间在哪儿？).
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: Speakers from the south usually say 哪里 (请问洗手间在哪里？); 哪儿 with the -r ending is typical of Beijing and the north. Both are standard and understood everywhere.

phrases.regional_note: Teaching sources say compass directions are typical of northern cities with grid-plan streets (e.g. Beijing), while in southern cities, with rivers and hills, people more often say left/right (and up/down). This is a widely repeated impression rather than a studied rule — in the south be ready for both.

rules.rule: Asking the way: [打扰一下，] 请问 + place + 在哪儿？ / 去 + place + 怎么走？ / 附近有 + place + 吗？ / place + 离这儿远吗？ Thank with 谢谢 or 好的，谢谢. Asking the way and understanding simple directions (direction, position, route, time) is an HSK level-1/level-2 task.
rules.why: All four question frames occur in official HSK/YCT dialogues; the 2025 HSK task syllabus lists 问路 (asking the way) and understanding 指路 (directions: 行进方向、位置、路线、时长、乘车信息) at levels 1-2.

rules.rule: 哪儿 and 哪里 both mean 'where' and are both HSK level-1 words; 现汉 labels 哪儿 as colloquial (〈口〉) and defines it as 哪里. Official dialogues use both for the same question (请问洗手间在哪儿？ / 请问，男洗手间在哪里？). The same pairing exists for 这儿/这里 'here' and 那儿/那里 'there'.
rules.why: 2025 HSK vocabulary syllabus (哪里 nǎlǐ, 哪儿 nǎr, level 1); 现汉 entries 哪儿 and 那儿 (〈口〉).
rules.regional_note: The -r (儿化) forms 哪儿 / 这儿 / 那儿 / 一点儿 are typical of Beijing and northern speech; southern speakers usually avoid them and say 哪里, 这里, 那里 and 一点 (some Southwestern Mandarin areas such as Chengdu and Chongqing do use -r). From a south/central-China family you are likely to hear 哪里 / 这里 / 一点 more often; both sets are standard. In native-speaker dialogue corpora 哪里 outnumbers 哪儿 about 8 to 1, and 这里 outnumbers 这儿 about 9 to 1.

phrases.usage: Telling the driver to stop when you recognise the place, and checking it is the right spot (YCT 4 sample dialogue in a car). 停车 alone = 'stop (the car)'; 吧 turns the second part into a 'right?' check. Slot: 学校东门 (your landmark). 这儿 and 这里 both mean 'here'. A bare 停车 sounds abrupt to a taxi driver; the polite way is 师傅，停在这里就好了 (travel.taxi.stop-here-is-fine).
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 这儿 (zhèr) is the northern, Beijing-style form; in south and central China people mostly say 这里 (zhèlǐ). Both are understood everywhere. Southern form: 停车，这里就是学校东门吧？

phrases.hanzi: 你还是开慢点儿吧，注意安全。
phrases.pinyin: Nǐ háishi kāi màn diǎnr ba, zhùyì ānquán.
phrases.literal: you had-better drive slow a-bit PART, pay-attention safety
phrases.english: You'd better drive a bit slower — safety first.
phrases.usage: Asking a driver to slow down; 还是……吧 = 'you'd better …'. HSK 5 sample, said to the driver on a motorway (the source begins 高速公路上， 'on the motorway', dropped here). To a taxi driver, start with 师傅.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: The -r (erhua) in 点儿 is northern; in south and central China people usually say 慢一点 / 慢点 (màn yīdiǎn / màn diǎn) without -r. Southern form: 你还是开慢一点吧。

rules.rule: In a metered taxi, ask for the receipt at the end (请给我一张发票 / 跟司机要发票) and keep it until you are sure you have all your things: it identifies the taxi, and in the HSK samples it carries the taxi company's phone number, which is how a bag left in the car is traced. For app rides (DiDi and similar), the trip record in the app shows the car, plate and driver, so contact the driver through the app.
rules.why: In the HSK 5 sample the friend of someone who left a bag in a taxi asks first about the receipt, because 发票上有出租车公司的电话; in an HSK 3 reading a traveller who left a suitcase in a taxi expects to find it because 我有出租车票. Dated practical detail: both are HSK 2.0-era papers. That the app shows the plate and car model is from the Beijing/Shanghai government DiDi guides.

rules.rule: Where to sit in a five-seat car: when the host drives you personally (a relative or colleague taking you out), the front passenger seat is the polite seat for the guest; in official/business reception with a driver, the seat behind the front passenger is the most polite seat, and the front passenger seat (随员座) is for an interpreter or secretary, so putting a guest there is impolite. For safety, the rear middle seat is safest, and everyone should wear a seat belt (系上安全带).
rules.why: HSK 6 sample reading 81-84 (citing experts): "在社交应酬中，如果是主人自驾车陪客人出去游玩，那么副驾驶座就是最有礼貌的座位。而在公务接待中，副驾驶座后面的座位是最礼貌的座位。公务接待时，副驾驶座被称为“随员座”，一般是翻译、秘书的位置，让客人坐在这里是不礼貌的。" Relevant when family or business contacts pick you up. These are conventions, not fixed rules: if the host or an older relative tells you where to sit, follow them.

rules.rule: Taxi vocabulary: 出租车 (taxi), 打车 (take a taxi), 叫车 (call a cab / request a ride in an app), 网约车 (app-based car), 滴滴 (DiDi). Colloquial alternatives: 打的 (take a taxi) and 的士 (taxi). Pronunciation of 的 in these words: CC-CEDICT gives dī (dǎdī, dīshì), which 现代汉语词典 says is how it is usually said in speech; the dictionary's standard reading is dí (dǎdí, díshì). CC-CEDICT also notes that in Taiwan 出租车 can mean 'rental car'.
rules.why: Knowing which word means what avoids confusion when ordering a ride or reading an app.
rules.regional_note: 现代汉语词典 labels 的士 〈方〉 (dialect origin) and 打的 〈口〉 (colloquial); 出租车 and 打车 are the neutral words everywhere in the mainland. CC-CEDICT marks the Taiwan meaning of 出租车 ('rental car').

rules.rule: Expect to pay by phone: Alipay (支付宝) or WeChat Pay (微信支付) by scanning a QR code (扫码, an HSK word). Since 2024 the authorities have pushed hotels, big shopping areas and tourist sites to accept foreign bank cards, and the payment apps have simplified sign-up and linking a card for foreigners; larger shopping areas and tourist sites must also take cash, and in Shenzhen, for example, banks have handed small shops and taxi drivers packs of change (零钱包). So set up a payment app before the trip, and carry some small RMB notes as a back-up.
rules.why: Paying is the last step of every taxi ride and hotel stay. CCTV 新闻联播 reported the People's Bank of China rule (1 Mar 2024: 规模以上商圈、旅游景区等必须支持移动支付、银行卡、现金等多样化支付方式) and the measures for foreign visitors (14 Apr 2024: 境外银行卡受理…酒店等重点场所; 零钱包 for 出租车司机; 支付平台也简化了注册、绑卡等流程). Dated: status as reported in 2024; the details of linking a foreign card are in the travel-facts topic (payments findings). The older HSK 5 dialogue 我们这里只能用现金付款 (cash only) shows an earlier situation and is not a guide to 2026.

rules.rule: Carry your destination in Chinese characters — the hotel's business card, a screenshot of its Chinese address, or the address your partner's family sends — and show it: 师傅，我要去这个地址。 Do not rely on English names or pinyin. In ride-hailing apps the destination you choose is passed to the driver in Chinese. Pay what the meter or app shows; tipping is not customary.
rules.why: Drivers read Chinese addresses at a glance but often cannot read English or transliterated names; several travel guides give this as the first taxi tip (status of the guides: 2023-2026).

rules.rule: Ride-hailing (DiDi and similar apps): before getting in, compare the plate number (车牌号) and car model shown in the app with the car. The driver checks the last four digits of your phone number (手机尾号多少？) — say them in Chinese or show them on your screen.
rules.why: This is how both sides make sure the right passenger gets into the right car. The Beijing (2020) and Shanghai (2024) government visitor guides describe the four-digit check, and travel guides add the plate check; Chinese riders describe the tail-number question as the driver's routine first words.

phrases.english: Excuse me, where is the waiting room?
phrases.usage: Adapted (slot change): the HSK 3 sample has 请问，二零四房间在哪儿？; the place noun is replaced by 候车室, CC-CEDICT 'waiting room (for train, bus etc)'. Large stations also call it 候车厅 (waiting hall). Other places for the slot: 检票口 (ticket gate), 售票处 (ticket office), 站台 (platform).

phrases.regional_note: 哪儿 (nǎr) is the northern erhua form; in south and central China people mostly say 哪里 (nǎlǐ). Both are understood everywhere. Southern form: 请问，候车室在哪里？

rules.rule: High-speed train seats (高铁/动车) are sold by class: 二等座 (second class, the cheaper standard choice) and 一等座 (first class); the seller asks 您想要一等座还是二等座？ CC-CEDICT also lists the classes of conventional trains: 硬座 (hard seat), 硬卧 (hard sleeper), 软卧 (soft sleeper).
rules.why: In the RiSAWOZ train dialogues the agent offers exactly these two classes and 二等座 is the cheaper one in the examples seen (e.g. 二等座134.5元 vs 一等座229.5元 for one Shanghai–Nanjing train in the 2020 dataset; illustrative, not current fares).

rules.rule: Bring the passport you booked with: you enter the station and board with it. The automatic gates are built for Chinese ID cards (and, since late 2023, the new foreign permanent-residence ID card); a foreign passport may not open them. If the gate does not take your passport, go to the staffed lane (人工通道; CCTV calls the staffed ticket gates 人工检票口) and show it: 这是我的护照。 Allow extra time for this.
rules.why: Railway notices from Nov 2023 extend self-service gate checks to holders of the new permanent-residence card “like mainland residents” and say nothing about ordinary passports; no 2025-2026 announcement opening the gates to passports was found. Some large stations may read passports at their gates, so treat this as station-dependent (status 2026-11).

phrases.hanzi: 你好，这儿可以用信用卡吗？
phrases.pinyin: Nǐ hǎo, zhèr kěyǐ yòng xìnyòngkǎ ma?
phrases.literal: hello, here can use credit-card Q
phrases.english: Hello, can I pay by credit card here?
phrases.usage: Asking how you can pay (HSK 5 sample wording). Swap the slot for the app you use: 这儿可以用支付宝吗？ / 这儿可以用微信吗？ Since 2024 hotels, big shopping areas and tourist sites have been pushed to accept foreign bank cards, but small shops and taxis mostly take mobile payment (or cash); see rule travel.taxi.rule.mobile-payment. In the 2.0-era HSK sample the answer was 'cash only' (我们这里只能用现金付款), which is not typical any more.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 这儿 (zhèr) is the northern, Beijing-style form; in south and central China people mostly say 这里 (zhèlǐ). Both are understood everywhere. Southern form: 这里可以用信用卡吗？

rules.rule: Hotel check-in follows a fixed pattern: you say what you booked and your surname (我前天订了一个标准间，我姓王); reception looks it up (您稍等，我查一下), asks for an ID document (请出示一下您的身份证) and does the check-in formalities (办理入住手续), then hands over the key card (这是您的房卡，请拿好).
rules.why: Knowing the steps makes the exchange predictable. For foreign guests the ID document is the passport; hotels must register foreign guests with the police, and since May 2024 they may not turn foreign guests away for lacking a special foreign-guest qualification (rule travel.hotel.rule.foreign-guests).

rules.rule: When you ring or approach staff about a problem, give your room number first (我住六零七 / 我住八零七), then what is wrong (……坏了), then the request (你能来看看吗？). Room numbers are read digit by digit, with 零 for zero.
rules.why: Two HSK sample dialogues with hotel staff follow exactly this order (我住六零七……空调坏了……你能来看看吗？ and 我住八零七……还有早饭吗？), which lets staff act at once.

rules.rule: Hotels must register foreign guests with the police, so reception will scan or copy your passport — that is normal. Since May 2024 the Ministry of Public Security, the Ministry of Commerce and the National Immigration Administration have told hotels to stop turning foreign guests away on the grounds that they lack a foreign-guest qualification (涉外资质). Local practice can still vary, so check the booking platform's note on foreign guests. If you stay with family instead of a hotel, the stay has to be registered with the local police (see the travel-facts topic).
rules.why: Before 2024 many budget hotels refused foreigners: Beijing hotel databases still listed 接待外宾 'accepts foreign guests' as a special feature (CrossWOZ, 2020: 这家酒店…没有接待外宾的服务). Dated: status of May 2024.

scenes.title: Restaurant: table, ordering, the bill
scenes.description: From being seated to ordering, spice level, drinks and extra rice, calling staff, asking for the bill and taking leftovers home. Includes the lines staff say to you, so dialogues can be built.

phrases.english: Excuse me! (calling the waiter or waitress)
phrases.usage: The standard, neutral way to call restaurant staff of either sex; the HSK papers use it constantly (服务员，请给我来一杯热水). Say it at normal volume with a raised hand or eye contact; a learner guide warns that shouting it across a crowded room can come across as rude, and native Zhihu answers say a simple 你好 or a wave also works. Younger staff are often called 美女 (to a woman) or 帅哥 (to a man): common and friendly but casual, and only for young staff (older staff: 阿姨 etc.). Do not call a waitress 小姐 (dated, and it has picked up a pejorative sense; see rule travel.restaurant.rule.calling-staff). Staff usually answer 好的 and come over (HSK: 好的，您要什么菜？).
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: Sichuan: a 2011 China Daily report on a Sichuan poll found most netizens preferred 妹儿 / 小妹儿 for young waitresses over a proposed new term 餐姐; as a visitor, 服务员 or 你好 is always safe.

phrases.pinyin: Nín hǎo! Huānyíng guānglín. Qǐngwèn nín jǐ wèi?
phrases.literal: you(polite) good! welcome come. may-I-ask you how-many (measure word for people)?
phrases.english: Hello, welcome! How many of you?
phrases.usage: What the host says when you walk in (HSK 5 listening script; the BCT business sample has 欢迎光临！请问几位用餐？). 位 is the polite measure word for people. Answer with the number: 我们两个人, or just 三个 as the HSK customer does (三个，我们提前预订了 'three, we booked'). If you booked they ask 您怎么称呼？ ('your name?') and lead you in with 里面请 ('this way, please').

phrases.literal: you(polite) are at here have-meal, or for you pack take-away?
phrases.english: Will you eat here, or shall we pack it for you to take away?
phrases.usage: Counter staff ask this, e.g. in fast-food places. Answer 在这儿吃 ("eat here") or 打包 / 带走 ("to go"). 用餐 is the more formal word for "have a meal" (XDHYCD), typical of staff talk. Only 内用 ("to eat in") is marked Taiwanese (CC-CEDICT), so skip the Taiwan question 內用還是外帶 that some phrasebooks give.
phrases.speaker: them
phrases.regional_note: Taiwan: 內用 / 外帶 ("for here / to go"; CC-CEDICT marks 内用 as Taiwanese). Mainland: 在这儿吃 / 打包 / 带走; 堂食 / 外带 are also mainland words (CC-CEDICT, no regional label).

phrases.english: Mild, medium or hot?
phrases.usage: What staff ask in hot-pot, Sichuan and Hunan restaurants; menus and delivery apps such as 美团 and 饿了么 show the same scale: 不辣 · 微辣 · 中辣 · 特辣 (some write 重辣). Answer 微辣 ("mild") or 不辣 ("not spicy"); learner sites suggest 微辣，我不太能吃辣. Listen carefully: 中辣 zhōnglà ("medium", first tone) and 重辣 zhònglà ("very hot", fourth tone) sound alike. CC-CEDICT: 微辣 "mildly spicy", 中辣 "medium level of spiciness", 重辣 "very spicy".

rules.rule: Call staff with 服务员 (neutral, any age or sex) or simply 你好 with a raised hand. 美女 / 帅哥 are common and friendly but casual: use them only for young staff, and age terms such as 阿姨 for older staff. Do not call a waitress 小姐.
rules.why: Native Zhihu answers: 小姐 replaced 服务员 as a polite term in the 1980s-90s, but the word later took on a pejorative meaning and is no longer widely used; 美女/帅哥 fit young people whose age you can't judge, older people are 阿姨/大爷; when unsure use 服务员, 你好 or a wave. Learner guides add that in Shanghai calling 帅哥/美女 is quite normal. The 2009-2010 HSK papers still have customers address shop staff as 小姐, so textbooks lag behind current use.
rules.regional_note: Sichuan: 妹儿 / 小妹儿 for young waitresses (China Daily 2011, Sichuan netizen poll). Shanghai: 帅哥 / 美女 widely used (learner guides).

rules.rule: Tipping is not customary in mainland China: do not add a tip in ordinary restaurants; it may even be refused. Some upscale restaurants add a service charge (服务费, CC-CEDICT 'service charge; cover charge') to the bill instead.
rules.why: China Daily (2016): 'tipping is not widely practiced on the Chinese mainland'; Shanghai restaurants that tried QR-code tips (usually 3-5 yuan) met resistance because tipping isn't a must. Learner guides: tipping is not customary and may be refused. Tatoeba: 中国人没有给小费的习惯. GoEast notes some upscale restaurants add a service charge; China Daily's government-services travel page says a service charge is generally added to the final bill in restaurants. XDHYCD defines 小费 as money customers give service staff on top of the bill.
rules.regional_note: Shanghai: some restaurants experimented with QR-code tipping (China Daily 2016).

phrases.english: I'm vegetarian.
phrases.usage: The standard way to say you are vegetarian (The Chairman's Bao: 请不要放肉，我吃素; Tatoeba: 我是吃素的, 我是素食主义者). XDHYCD defines 吃素 as not eating fish, meat etc., adding that for Buddhists it also excludes scallions and garlic (the "five pungent" vegetables, 五荤). LTL goes further and says 我吃素 also rules out eggs and dairy, but people's understanding varies, so say exactly what you do and don't eat. Vegan: 我是纯素食者 (Tatoeba). Learner guides list chicken stock, meat broth and lard separately, so name them if they matter (请不要用猪油和肉汤).

rules.rule: 吃素 ("vegetarian") means not eating meat or fish; in the Buddhist sense it also excludes the "five pungent" vegetables (五荤: onion, garlic, scallion, chives, leeks). LTL says it also rules out eggs and dairy, but people's understanding varies. Say precisely what you avoid (我不吃肉 / 请不要用猪油和肉汤; vegan: 我是纯素食者) and ask about each dish (这个是荤的还是素的？).
rules.why: XDHYCD: 吃素 = 不吃鱼、肉等食物，佛教徒的吃素戒律还包括不吃葱蒜等; 荤 sense ❷ = 佛教徒称葱蒜等有特殊气味的菜：五荤. LTL: 我吃素 is a Buddhist term (no meat, eggs, dairy or 五荤); saying 'I'm vegetarian' is often not enough, say 'I don't eat meat' and ask twice about meat, fish, eggs and milk products. Tatoeba: 我是纯素食者 = "I am vegan". XDHYCD 荤 ❶ example: 饺子馅儿是荤的还是素的？.

rules.rule: A "vegetable" dish can still contain meat garnish, meat in the sauce, meat or chicken stock, fish sauce, lard or chicken bouillon powder (鸡精). Ask about each dish (这个菜有没有肉？ / 这个是荤的还是素的？), say what not to cook with (请不要用猪油和肉汤), repeat the request, and check the dish when it arrives.
rules.why: Hutong School: when asking for a dish without meat, more often than not some small pieces of meat end up on top; meat is used as a garnish and seen as a sign of prosperity; its vegan sentence names chicken stock, meat broth, fish stock, fish sauce and lard. LTL: ask twice. Learner guides: hidden fish sauce or chicken broth; many dishes contain some meat even if the menu doesn't say so. CLI: a server may insist a tofu dish is vegetarian although its sauce uses beef, and a pumpkin soup may be made with pork-bone stock. XDHYCD: 鸡精 is made from chicken meat, egg, chicken bones and MSG; 高汤 is stock boiled from meat or poultry.

rules.rule: Spice levels are relative to the region: Sichuan food is known for being numbing and hot (麻 and 辣), 微辣 ('mild') in Sichuan or Chongqing can still be very hot, and in Hunan even dishes ordered 不要放辣 may come out spicy. If you can't take chili, say 我怕辣, ask 这个菜辣吗？ and choose dishes that are not chili-based.
rules.why: The Paper (also on Zhihu): a netizen on a Sichuan forum stressed 微辣 repeatedly and was still 'burned'; a Guangdong netizen says Guangdong 'mild' is a small piece of chili while Sichuan 'mild' can be a whole one, and people's sense of spice levels is subjective. Zhihu: relatives from Zhejiang ordered 不要放辣 in a Hunan restaurant and found every dish spicy (chili on the wok). Popular saying: 重庆火辣，四川麻辣，湖南香辣; Sichuan's numbing 麻 comes from Sichuan pepper (花椒). HSK 5 reading: 川菜的突出特点是麻和辣.
rules.regional_note: The sources name Sichuan, Chongqing and Hunan; what counts as 'mild' depends on the region (a Guangdong 'mild' is far milder than a Sichuan one).

rules.rule: Halal restaurants are marked 清真: they serve no pork and usually no alcohol; many are run by Chinese Muslims from the northwest and are known for lamb skewers and hand-pulled noodles (拉面). When ordering for Hui or Uyghur guests, avoid pork.
rules.why: That's Mandarin: 清真饮食 excludes pork and alcohol. ChinesePod's halal lesson: the restaurant doesn't sell alcohol. Hutong School food guides: qīngzhēn restaurants are commonly run by Chinese Muslims, mostly from the northwest, with lamb skewers and lāmiàn (拉面). Zhihu banquet guide: 回族、维吾尔族不吃猪肉. XDHYCD: 清真 = 伊斯兰教的 (清真寺, 清真餐厅). CrossWOZ dialogues name restaurants such as 清真长顺牛肉馆 and 清真回民饭馆.

rules.rule: Bargaining is expected at markets, street and night-market stalls, antique and tourist stalls; in modern shopping malls prices are set and not negotiable. Open with 太贵了 / 可以便宜一点吗？ and be ready to walk away (我不要了). Bargaining is 砍价 (colloquial) or 讲价 (XDHYCD).
rules.why: Learner guides: modern shopping malls generally have set prices that can't be negotiated, while vendors at night markets, antique stalls or personal booths usually expect customers to question their prices; bargaining is most expected in street markets and tourist shops; 我不要了 signals you are walking away and often brings a better offer. The HSK 3 script shows a seller offering 便宜五十块 after 太贵了.

rules.rule: Paying by phone (Alipay 支付宝 or WeChat Pay 微信) is so common that many people no longer carry cash or cards. Either you scan the merchant's QR code (我扫你) or the cashier scans the payment code in your app (你扫我); if your phone has no data, ask the merchant to scan you (你可以扫我吗？).
rules.why: BCT sample (CLEC): mobile payment has become a new way to pay and many people no longer carry cash or credit cards. LTL: 我扫你还是你扫我 is heard often; GoEast: 付款码 = payment code; LTL Alipay FAQ: ask the merchant to scan you when you have no data.

rules.rule: If you need an official receipt (发票, fapiao) for expenses, ask for it when you pay: it is often not offered unless you ask, but by law the business that receives the payment must issue one (Invoice Management Measures Art. 18). For a company fapiao give the company name and its tax number; refusals can be reported to the tax hotline 12366.
rules.why: China Briefing: the consumer is responsible for requesting the fapiao because it is not always offered; businesses are obliged to issue one on request at the time of purchase; refusals can be reported (tax hotline 12366); a company-type fapiao carries the buyer's company name and tax registration number (also address and bank account).

rules.rule: Emergency numbers in mainland China: 110 police, 119 fire, 120 ambulance (pre-hospital medical emergency). Dial the three digits directly.
rules.why: Android's emergency-number database lists CN 110 POLICE, 120 AMBULANCE, 119 FIRE. Chinese regulations name the same numbers: Hangzhou (2014): citizens who find a seriously ill or injured person may call 120; Shanghai: the 110 police alarm number; Sichuan (2021): the 119 fire alarm line; Hainan (2026): witnesses should call 110, 119, 120 and other dedicated lines. A survival-phrase guide lists 救护车 120, 警察 110, 火警 119.

rules.rule: At a Chinese hospital you register first (挂号) at the registration windows: ask for 普通挂号 (ordinary registration) for a normal consultation; first-time patients get a hospital card (就诊卡). For injuries or a high fever go straight to the emergency department (急诊), which usually needs no booking.
rules.why: XDHYCD: 看病要先挂号 ('to see a doctor you must first register'). That's Mandarin: look for the 挂号 sign at the registration windows, ask for 普通挂号 (you get a numbered slip), and a 就诊卡 is needed for first-time visits. ChinesePod: in Chinese cities you can usually go straight to emergency care for injuries or high fever without booking. HSK 5 script: 去皮肤科看看吧，您去那边挂号.

situations.title: Family
situations.intro: Meeting and visiting your partner's family: forms of address, gifts, dinner, small talk and festivals.

scenes.title: Meeting your partner's parents: what to call them and what to say
scenes.description: How to address your partner's parents before marriage (叔叔/阿姨, or 伯父/伯母) and after the wedding (改口 to 爸/妈, usually at the wedding tea ceremony, with the 改口费 gift), short polite lines for a first visit, and what the hosts will say to you.

phrases.english: Uncle — what you call your partner's father (or any man of your parents' generation) before you are married
phrases.usage: Before marriage a friend's or partner's parents are 叔叔 and 阿姨: in the official HSK 3 sample paper a man about to marry tells a friend '让叔叔、阿姨也一起来' (bring your parents — lit. uncle and auntie — along too). CC-CEDICT: 'form of address used by children for a male one generation older'; Xinhua: '泛称与父同辈而年龄较小的男子' (general term for men of one's father's generation who are younger [than one's father]); for a man clearly older than your own father the matching title is 伯父/伯伯. Pair it with 您: HSK 3 sample '叔叔，您愿意教我吗？'. Children will in turn call you 叔叔 if you are a man of their parents' generation. Whether your partner's family expects 叔叔 or 伯父 is not settled by these sources: ask your partner.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Auntie — what you call your partner's mother (or any woman of your parents' generation) before you are married
phrases.usage: The counterpart of 叔叔 (HSK 3 sample: '让叔叔、阿姨也一起来'). Xinhua: '称呼跟母亲辈分相同、年纪差不多的妇女：王～' (address for a woman of one's mother's generation and similar age, e.g. 王阿姨); CC-CEDICT: 'woman of similar age to one's parents (term of address used by child)'. HSK 5 sample: '阿姨，您现在还每天看书吗？' (a young man to a retired woman, with 您). 阿姨 is also how nannies and childcare workers are addressed (Xinhua sense ③; CC-CEDICT 'childcare worker; nursemaid'). Alternative pair: 伯父/伯母.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: Xinhua marks only the kinship sense 'mother's sister' as dialectal (〈方〉); the title sense (王阿姨) has no regional label.

phrases.english: Sorry to bother you. / Sorry for the trouble.
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'sorry to interrupt you, but ... / sorry to have bothered you / sorry, I have to go'. In the HSK 4 sample a visitor who did not find the person ends with '好的，那我过一会儿再联系吧，打扰了，再见。'. So it fits when you interrupt someone and when you take your leave after imposing on them. CC-CEDICT also lists a slang sense (coined c. 2017, mostly online): said facetiously to end a conversation with someone insufferable — your tone makes the difference.

phrases.english: Your grandpa looks very young.
phrases.usage: Compliment from the YCT 4 sample ('你爷爷看上去很年轻。' — reply: '他身体不错，每天都坚持散步两个小时。'), said to your partner about a relative; swap the relative (slot). 看起来 works the same way (Tatoeba: '她看起来很年轻。'). To the person directly: 阿姨，您看起来真年轻！ (separate item). 你妈 is normal inside a sentence (Tatoeba: '你和你妈用上海话聊天的时候…'), but as a bare exclamation it is a curse (CC-CEDICT), so 你妈妈 sounds gentler when you speak of your partner's mother. CC-CEDICT 看上去: 'it would appear; it seems (that)'.

phrases.english: Uncle (respectful) — title for a man of your father's generation who is older than your own father
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'father's elder brother; term of respect for older man'. As a title it strictly suits a man older than your own father (Xinhua defines 叔叔 as the term for the younger ones). HSK 2025 lists 伯父/伯伯/伯母 at level 7-9 and 叔叔/阿姨 at level 3. Whether your partner's family prefers 伯父/伯母 or 叔叔/阿姨 at a first visit is not settled by these sources: ask your partner.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: As a title for a partner's father, 伯父 is understood everywhere. Don't carry over the northern kinship word 大爷 (= your own father's older brother in the north; see the paternal chart): said to an unrelated man, 大爷 is a title for an old man (现代汉语词典 大爷 ❷ '尊称年长的男子').

phrases.english: Mum — how you address your partner's mother once you are married
phrases.usage: After the wedding you 改口 (change how you address them): CC-CEDICT 改口 '…as when one marries and starts to call one's husband's parents 爸爸 and 妈妈'; 改口费 is given to the new daughter-in-law or son-in-law, so the switch concerns both. 妈 is the everyday short form; with 您 it stays respectful, as in the HSK 4 sample '妈，您的手机响了。'. phrases.english: 'change-of-address money': a cash gift from the parents to their new son- or daughter-in-law at the wedding
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'a gift of money given by parents on both sides after a wedding, to their new daughter-in-law or son-in-law'. As the name says (改口 + 费 'fee'), it goes with 改口: the parents hand it over when you first call them 爸/妈, typically after you serve them tea at the wedding (改口茶). There is no fixed amount; the two families agree on it, often choosing a lucky number.
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: Who gives it varies: in many places it is the groom's parents giving it to the bride, while in some places (reportedly especially North China) the bride's parents also give it to the groom. Ask your partner what their family and region expect.

rules.rule: Speak to your partner's parents (and other elders) with 您, the courteous 'you', and put their title first: 叔叔，您…; 阿姨，您好. After marriage 您 stays respectful (妈，您…), but follow your partner's lead: many families, especially in the south, say 你 to their own parents.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT: 您 = 'you (courteous, as opposed to informal 你)'. The official HSK samples show younger speakers pairing titles with 您: '叔叔，您愿意教我吗？', '阿姨，您现在还每天看书吗？', '妈，您的手机响了。', '爸，您为什么要问我这么简单的问题？'. (Some samples show children using 你 with their own parents, e.g. the answer option '爸爸，你累了吧'; for an in-law, 您 is the courteous form.)
rules.regional_note: 您 is far more frequent in northern speech (Beijing above all); in the south many people say 你 even to elders in everyday talk, so 您 can sound a little formal there — but it is never wrong at a first meeting (anecdotal evidence: learner-forum reports).

rules.rule: Before marriage — and especially before you are engaged — call your partner's parents by kinship titles, as you would a friend's parents: 叔叔 (father) and 阿姨 (mother), greeting them with 叔叔阿姨好; or 伯父/伯母 if they are older than your own parents. Surname + title (王阿姨, 张叔叔) is the standard pattern for other older acquaintances, such as neighbours and family friends.
rules.why: HSK 3 sample: a man invites a friend's parents to his wedding as '叔叔、阿姨'. Xinhua: 阿姨 = '称呼跟母亲辈分相同、年纪差不多的妇女'; 叔叔 = '泛称与父同辈而年龄较小的男子'. CC-CEDICT: 伯父 'term of respect for older man', 伯母 'polite form of address for a woman who is about the age of one's mother'. HSK 2025 syllabus: '姓氏+亲属称谓（张爷爷）'.

rules.rule: 改口: you switch to 爸/妈 (爸爸/妈妈) for your partner's parents at the wedding, usually during the tea ceremony (敬茶, also called 改口茶), and they give you 改口费. Before that use 叔叔/阿姨 (or 伯父/伯母), and don't start saying 爸/妈 on your own initiative: some parents invite it earlier (after the engagement or the marriage registration), and then you follow their lead.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT 改口: '…to change the way one addresses sb (as when one marries and starts to call one's husband's parents 爸爸 and 妈妈)'; 改口费: 'a gift of money given by parents on both sides after a wedding, to their new daughter-in-law or son-in-law'. 现代汉语词典/Xinhua 改口 ②: '改变称呼'. Web articles (search summaries): '敬茶又叫"改口茶"…当双方父母喝下新人们敬的茶后，还会给新人们改口费'; '若是两人还没有开始谈婚论嫁…就喊叔叔阿姨是最好的' (maigoo); parents who accept you may say you can call them 爸/媽 (Marie Claire Taiwan); following one's spouse in calling the in-laws 爸爸/媽媽 is still widespread (ETtoday, 2026).
rules.regional_note: Who gives 改口费, and how much, varies by region and family — in some places (reportedly especially North China) the bride's parents also give it to the groom. Ask your partner.

rules.rule: Kinship words double as polite titles for people who are not relatives: 叔叔/阿姨 for your parents' generation, surname + 爷爷 (张爷爷) for the grandparents' generation, 大哥/大姐 for people somewhat older than you, 大叔/大姨 for people about your parents' age.
rules.why: HSK 2025 syllabus: '姓氏+亲属称谓（张爷爷）'. Xinhua: 爷爷 sense 3 '对男性尊长的称呼'. CC-CEDICT: 大哥 'polite address for a man of about the same age as oneself', 大姐 'polite term of address for a girl or woman slightly older than the speaker', 大叔 'term used to address a man about the age of one's father', 大姨 'respectful term of address for a woman who is about the age of one's mother', 大娘 'aunt (polite address)'.
rules.regional_note: relationship.js readme: 大爷 can mean grandfather's elder brother or, in the north, father's elder brother. CC-CEDICT 大爷 dàye is also a 'term of respect for older man' — but dàyé (full second tone) means 'arrogant idler'.

scenes.title: First visit: arriving and giving gifts
scenes.description: Arriving at your partner's parents' home for the first time: greeting them, what to bring and what not to bring, handing over gifts modestly with both hands, the ritual refusal exchange, and being offered tea.

phrases.english: Hello, Uncle! Hello, Auntie! (greeting your partner's father and mother)
phrases.usage: Greeting pattern "(称谓)+好！" (address term + 好) from the official function list, section 打招呼 (greeting). 叔叔 and 阿姨 are the dictionary-standard ways to address a man / a woman of your parents' generation who is not your relative; an HSK 3 sample dialogue uses 叔叔、阿姨 for (most likely) a friend's parents. Say it when you arrive, before handing over gifts. Slot: the address term; check with your partner which term the family expects (see the address-term rule below).
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: XDHYCD: strictly 叔叔 is for men younger than your own father and 伯伯/伯父 for men older than him; which term this family expects is a family/regional habit not researched here: ask your partner.

slots.meaning: address term (称谓) for the person you greet

phrases.english: Just a small token (of my regard).
phrases.usage: A fixed modest formula listed in the official function list under 14. 馈赠 (gift-giving); say it as you hand over the gift, often after 这是送给您的. XDHYCD defines 心意 as "对人的情意" (kind feelings towards someone). The same list gives a much more formal "……，不成敬意，请笑纳" (it is not much, please accept it), and XDHYCD calls 笑纳 a 客套话 for asking someone to accept a gift. the attested forms are 一点儿心意 and 一点儿小意思.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: The 儿 is optional (XDHYCD writes 一点（儿））. Erhua is mainly a northern habit: with a south/central-China family you will mostly hear 一点心意, and in typed native dialogue 一点 without 儿 is the norm. Both are correct.

phrases.hanzi: 这是我的一点儿小意思。
phrases.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ de yīdiǎnr xiǎoyìsi.
phrases.english: This is just a little something from me.
phrases.usage: XDHYCD 小意思 sense ❶: "微薄的心意（款待宾客或赠送礼物时的客气话）" = a polite formula used when entertaining guests or giving presents; its example is "这是我的一点儿～，送给你做个纪念。" (the phrase here is the first clause). phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 儿 optional, as above; in the south you will mostly hear 这是我的一点小意思. Careful: 小意思 on its own also means “no big deal” (e.g. as a reply to thanks).

phrases.literal: please accept this (measure word) small gift BA
phrases.english: Please accept this little gift.
phrases.usage: Use it to insist gently when the hosts protest that you should not have brought anything. 收下 is the verb for finally accepting a gift (XDHYCD 客气 example: “他客气了一番，把礼物收下了” — he made polite protests, then accepted the gift). phrases.hanzi: 这是我从荷兰带来的特产，您尝尝吧。
phrases.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ cóng Hélán dàilái de tèchǎn, nín chángchang ba.
phrases.literal: this is I from Netherlands bring-come DE specialty, you (polite) taste-taste BA
phrases.english: This is a specialty I brought from the Netherlands, please try it.
phrases.usage: ADAPTED, not verbatim: the HSK 5 sample sentence is "这是我从海南带回来的特产，你尝尝吧。" (said by someone back from a trip to Hainan). Changes: place slot 海南 -> 荷兰; 你 -> 您; and 带回来 "brought back" -> 带来 "brought" (as in Tatoeba "从中国带来的龙井茶"), because XDHYCD defines 回来 as coming back to where one started — keep 带回来 only if you are returning home. XDHYCD: 特产 = a product special to a place or country, so it fits Dutch food specialties (尝尝 = have a taste; use it for food or drink only). phrases.literal: come just come MA, still bring what things!

phrases.usage: The ritual protest you will most likely hear when you hand over a gift. It means “having you here is what matters” (China News Service: 潜台词是“你人来了就好，不用送这送那的”) and is not a real refusal: keep offering (一点心意，您就收下吧！) and the gift will be accepted. phrases.regional_note: You may also hear 来就来呗 (呗 bei, another colloquial particle) with the same meaning.

phrases.hanzi: 你的心意我领了，但礼物无论如何不能收。
phrases.pinyin: Nǐ de xīnyì wǒ lǐng le, dàn lǐwù wúlùnrúhé bù néng shōu.
phrases.literal: your heart-intention I receive-LE, but gift in-any-case cannot accept
phrases.english: I appreciate the thought, but I really can't accept the gift.
phrases.usage: A firm, formal refusal, not the ritual protest: the official function list files it under 47. 拒绝 (declining), next to 这种礼物绝对不能收 (this kind of gift absolutely cannot be accepted), and 无论如何 means “in any case”. Dictionary variants: 我领这个情，但东西不能收 (XDHYCD 领情) and 您的美意，我心领了 (XDHYCD 心领: polite formula for declining a gift or a meal). It is what someone says who really must not accept (a teacher, an official) or when a gift is too expensive. On a family visit the protest you will usually hear is lighter: 来就来嘛，还带什么东西！ or 你太客气了！ (see those items). If you do hear this formula, do not keep pushing; ask your partner.

rules.rule: When you hand over a gift, your hosts will usually protest first (客气): 来就来嘛，还带什么东西！ (“just coming is enough — why bring anything?”), 你太客气了！, 下次别买了 (“don't buy anything next time”). This is a ritual: the real meaning is “having you here is what matters”, and a guest is still expected to bring something. Hosts may decline two or three times; keep offering warmly (一点心意 / 一点小意思, 您就收下吧！) until they accept. Fixed formulas such as 你的心意我领了，但礼物无论如何不能收 or 您的美意，我心领了 are different: they announce a real refusal.
rules.why: China News Service (2022) explains that 来就来呗 really means 你人来了就好，不用送这送那的; a teaching page models the exchange 一点小意思，你别嫌弃 — 哎呀，你太客气了，来就来嘛，还带什么东西！ and describes the first refusal as an opening move; a NetEase article lists 还拿东西干啥？ and 下次来可别买了 as host formulas not to take literally; a Shanghai etiquette wiki says the recipient may refuse 2 or 3 times while the giver insists (all seen as WebSearch summaries). The official 2002 function list files 你的心意我领了，但礼物无论如何不能收 under 47. 拒绝 (declining), next to 这种礼物绝对不能收; XDHYCD 客气❷: 他客气了一番，把礼物收下了.

rules.rule: Address your partner's parents with a title. The dictionary-standard titles for unrelated people of your parents' generation are 叔叔 (a man; strictly one younger than your own father) or 伯伯/伯父 (a man older than your father), and 阿姨 (a woman). Use 您 when you speak to them.
rules.why: XDHYCD defines 叔叔❷, 伯父❷ and 阿姨❷ as forms of address for non-relatives of the parents' generation; 您 is "你 (含敬意)", the respectful you.
rules.regional_note: In south and central China the maternal grandparents are usually 外婆/外公; 姥姥/姥爷 are the northern terms (the kinship library relationship.js lists 外婆/外公 first as the general forms and gives 姥姥/姥爷 in its 北方 locale). XDHYCD labels 外婆/外公 〈方〉 (dialectal), but in the south they are the everyday words. 您 is used much more in the north than in the south, but 您 to your partner's parents is polite everywhere. Titles can change after a wedding (改口, XDHYCD: 改变称呼, e.g. from 姐姐 to 嫂子): ask your partner what this family expects.

rules.rule: Typical gifts for a first visit to your partner's parents: fruit, tea, nutrition or health products (营养品, 补品 — choose them after asking about the parents' health), milk, and specialties from home (特产 — Dutch specialties fit well). Alcohol or cigarettes only if the father actually drinks or smokes, and then his usual brand. Bring something for both parents, not just for the father; even numbers are preferred (买双不买单); keep the value in line with the family's means. How many gifts are expected differs by region and family, so agree on it with your partner beforehand.
rules.why: one case shows a girlfriend's family asking for 18 items while the author thought six or eight were enough. XDHYCD: 补品 = 滋补身体的食品或药品; 特产 = a product special to a place or country.
rules.regional_note: Customs (number of gifts, money gifts, local specialties) vary strongly by region and family; ask your partner what their family expects.

rules.rule: Avoid these gifts because of how their names sound or what they stand for: a clock (送钟 sòng zhōng sounds like 送终 sòngzhōng, attending a dying elder or arranging their funeral — the classic taboo; sources disagree about watches, so avoid them for elders too); pears (梨 lí sounds like 离 lí “to part”) and umbrellas (伞 sǎn sounds like 散 sàn “to break up”), especially for a couple; shoes (鞋 xié sounds like 邪 xié “evil”); a green hat (戴绿帽子 means one's wife or partner is unfaithful); knives or scissors (cutting the relationship); white or black wrapping (colours of mourning — red and gold are festive); anything in fours (四 sì sounds like 死 sǐ “death”). Pairs and even numbers are preferred (“good things come in pairs”).
rules.why: English-language features in mainland media list the same taboos: People's Daily Online “Culture Insider: Taboos in gift-giving” (2015), China Daily “The art of giving to Chinese” (2015) and “Beware green hat gifts” (2008), The Beijinger (2020), and a Chinese Language Institute reader (seen as WebSearch summaries). The sound links are dictionary facts: XDHYCD 送终 = 长辈亲属临终时在身旁照料，也指安排长辈亲属的丧事; 戴绿帽子 = 称人妻子有外遇; 离 = 分离; 散 sàn = 由聚集而分离; 白事 = 丧事.
rules.regional_note: The sources date from 2008-2020; a Global Times story mentions a Chinese recipient who was happy with a clock, so younger urban people may be relaxed about some of these. For a first visit to elders, play safe.

rules.rule: Hand the gift over with both hands, and receive anything you are given with both hands. Do not expect it to be opened in front of you: traditionally a gift is put aside and opened after the guest has left, so that nobody loses face if it is not right — unless the giver insists or the people are already close. Chinese people who know Western customs may expect you to open a gift they give you straight away; either way is fine.
rules.why: Whether younger Chinese now usually open gifts on the spot is not documented in what was found.

phrases.english: I drove here today, so I can't drink.
phrases.usage: A standard reason for not drinking; then offer to toast with tea (我以茶代酒，敬您一杯). Wording from a learner dialogue (“我今天开车来的，不能喝酒。我以茶代酒，祝小王生日快乐！”); 我开车来的 “I came by car” is common in native-written dialogue (RiSAWOZ), and Tatoeba has the slogan 喝酒不开车，开车不喝酒. The 的 ending is the 是……的 pattern with 是 left out, stressing how you came.

rules.rule: Chopstick manners: while talking, do not wave your chopsticks around; do not tap bowls, plates or the table with them; never point at people with them; when you put them down during the meal, lay them on the table or on the edge of your plate and never stick them (upright) into the rice bowl; avoid making noise with them.
rules.why: Stated in an official HSK 5 reading passage: “筷子……在使用上也有很多讲究。用餐过程中，如果说话，不要将筷子随便晃动，也不要用筷子敲打碗、盘子以及桌面，更不能用筷子指点他人，暂时离开时，要把筷子轻轻放在桌子上或餐盘边，不能插在饭碗里，而且尽量不要发出响声。” (the keyed answer is “说话时敲筷子不礼貌”). For serving chopsticks (公筷) and hosts putting food in your bowl (夹菜), see the separate rule.

rules.rule: Hosts may urge you, repeatedly, to drink (劝酒) and to eat more. Decline with a short reason (我不会喝酒 / 开车不喝酒; 不了，我真的饱了) rather than a bare no.
rules.why: XDHYCD defines 劝酒 as "（酒席上）劝人喝酒" with the example "主人举杯频频劝酒" (the host raised his glass and kept urging people to drink), and 海量 ❷ has the urging line "您是～，不妨多喝几杯" (you can hold your drink, have a few more). Food urging appears in the YCT dialogue "别客气，再吃几个饺子吧 — 不了，我真的饱了". Giving a reason is advice drawn from the sample replies, not a stated rule.

rules.rule: Let the host seat you. The seat facing the door (the entrance) is the seat of honour (上座); at a family meal it normally goes to the most senior person or to whoever the host wants to honour, so do not take it yourself unless you are pressed to. Let the elders sit down first, and do not start eating until the most senior person at the table has picked up their chopsticks (you can invite them: 您先请).
rules.why: China Daily's table-etiquette guide (2024): “The seat facing the entrance is the most important and is usually reserved for the host or the guest of honor”; other guides say the guest of honour sits facing the door, in the 上座. The Paper (澎湃新闻) states the 长幼原则: 应当让年长的长辈首先就坐，然后年轻人再就坐, and 餐桌上辈分最高的人动筷之后，其他人才能动筷 (all seen as WebSearch summaries). XDHYCD: 上座 = the most honoured seat when seats are ranked; 让座❷ = the host inviting the guests to sit. The BCT sample keys 可随意就座 (sit anywhere) as not the right answer.
rules.regional_note: Guides differ on details (host vs. guest of honour in the seat facing the door), and families differ: follow the host's arrangement.

rules.rule: Leaving has a fixed exchange: the host sees you out and says 您慢走 / 您走好; you ask them not to come further (别送了 / 您留步), and they may still walk you to the bus stop.
rules.why: Official function list, section 告别: "[主人]：不远送了 [主人]：您慢走/您走好 [客人]：别送了/您留步"; XDHYCD 留步 is a 客套话 used when the host sees the guest off; HSK 5 dialogue in which the host insists on walking the guest to the bus stop.

rules.rule: Hosts may put food into your bowl or onto your plate (夹菜) to look after you: accept some and thank them; if it becomes too much, 不用不用，我自己来 or 够了，谢谢您！我吃饱了. Since 2020 many Chinese cities have promoted serving chopsticks and spoons (公筷公勺), and restaurants were asked to provide them; at home many families still take food from shared dishes with their own chopsticks, and some feel that serving chopsticks between family members are 见外 (treating each other as outsiders). If serving chopsticks are on the table, use them to take food from shared dishes and to serve others.
rules.why: XDHYCD 布菜 = 把菜肴分给座上的客人 (the host serving dishes to the seated guests); YCT/HSK dialogues show hosts urging food (别客气，再吃几个饺子吧; 再来点儿米饭吧，你吃得太少了). 公筷: Beijing News (2020) reports local regulations and proposals across China calling for 公筷公勺; a People's Daily group paper (2020) tells of a family switching to them; a health-news article names the resistance (“用公筷公勺就是见外”, “一家人吃饭还用公勺公筷太麻烦”) and a Shanghai survey with 92% approval (attitude, not use); an overseas Chinese paper notes serving chopsticks come out when guests visit (all seen as WebSearch summaries). CC-CEDICT 公筷 = serving chopsticks.
rules.regional_note: Practice varies by family; watch what your partner's family does.

rules.rule: You do not have to drain every glass. If you drink alcohol, you can empty your glass when you toast an elder and say 我干了，您随意 (“I'll finish mine, you drink as you like”). If you do not drink, give a reason (我今天开车来的，不能喝酒 — driving is a standard reason) and toast with tea or juice: 我以茶代酒，敬您一杯. Avoid 我就喝一点 (“just a little”), which invites endless top-ups, and do not say 我干了，您随意 while drinking tea.
rules.why: 我酒量不好 / 我开车 are the usual reasons and 以茶代酒 is an accepted alternative; one commenter warns about 我就喝一点 and about combining 以茶代酒 with 我干了你随意. XDHYCD 干杯 = 喝干杯中的酒; 随意 = 任凭自己的意思.
rules.regional_note: Drinking culture (how hard hosts press, 劝酒) varies by region and family; not researched here.

phrases.english: Good morning! (to an elder)
phrases.usage: Morning greeting with the respectful 您, e.g. when you see your partner's parents in the morning during a stay. Listed in the official greeting list; XDHYCD uses "老师，您早！" as its example for 您. Neutral alternative: 早上好！
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 您早 is a typically northern (Beijing) greeting, and 您 is used less in the south; with a south/central-China family the neutral 早上好！ (or just 早！) may sound more natural.

phrases.english: Have you eaten? (a greeting)
phrases.usage: A greeting, not an invitation: the official list files it under 打招呼 (greeting), marked “[吃饭前后]” (around mealtimes) and “以下多用于中国人之间” (mostly used between Chinese people). The same list notes the habit of greeting by asking about what the other person is evidently doing (上课去呀？ / 去哪儿了？ / 回来啦！). Today you hear it mostly from older people and between neighbours or acquaintances; many younger urban people just say 你好 or “hi”. Answer briefly and return it: 吃了，您呢？ (or 我吃过了。 / 我还没吃。).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: How much do you earn a month?
phrases.usage: Adapted from Tatoeba “他一个月赚多少？” (How much does he earn per month?) with the person slot 他 -> 你. Relatives do ask about income at family gatherings (New Year features in Chinese media list it among the awkward questions; a Taiwanese analysis calls it the hardest one — say little and you are looked down on, say a lot and you are showing off). A vague answer such as 还可以 and a change of subject is the usual way out; see the rule on personal questions.

phrases.regional_note: XDHYCD labels 赚 in the sense “to earn (wages)” as dialectal (〈方〉) and gives 挣钱 as the standard word, so in the north you will often hear 你一个月挣多少？ (zhèng). Both are understood everywhere.

phrases.english: Let's talk about that later.
phrases.usage: Soft way to put off a question or request; listed under 拒绝 (declining) in the official list, and XDHYCD 再说❶ = “表示留待以后办理或考虑” (leave it to be dealt with or considered later). phrases.english: You flatter me. / That's too kind.
phrases.usage: Modest answer to a compliment. XDHYCD: 过奖 = 谦辞 “used when the other person praises you”, example “您～了，我不过做了该做的事。”; the official list of modest replies (谦虚) has 过奖了; Tatoeba “过奖了。” = “I'm flattered.” Still common and polite today, especially to elders, and a little formal; native-written dialogue has “谢谢，您过奖了……”. A plain 谢谢 (often with a modest note, e.g. 谢谢，我还在学习) is also fine.

phrases.usage: The textbook modest reply to praise: XDHYCD 哪里❺ “谦辞，用来婉转地推辞对自己的褒奖” with the exchange “你这篇文章写得真好！” — “哪里，哪里！”; in the official 谦虚 list; the keyed answer to “大家都说你是公司里最好的员工” in an official BCT sample; Tatoeba “哪里哪里！”. rules.rule: 吃了吗？ (“Have you eaten?”) around mealtimes is a greeting, not an invitation; greeting someone by asking about what they are evidently doing (上课去呀？ “off to class?”, 去哪儿了？ “where have you been?”, 回来啦！ “you're back!”) works the same way. Today it is heard mostly from older people and between neighbours or acquaintances; many younger urban people just say 你好 or “hi”. Answer briefly and return it: 吃了，您呢？ (or 我吃过了。 / 我还没吃。).
rules.why: The official 2002 function list files these under 1. 打招呼 (greeting) with the notes “[吃饭前后]” (before/after meals), “[估计对方作什么就问什么]” (ask about what you guess the other person is doing) and “以下多用于中国人之间” (mostly used between Chinese people). Current usage: Language Log (only between people who know each other; young people may just say hi), The World of Chinese and GoEast Mandarin (typical of the older generation; not an invitation; usual reply 吃了，你呢？), seen as WebSearch summaries.

rules.rule: Use 您 (nín, respectful "you") with your partner's parents, grandparents and other elders; they will usually call you 你.
rules.why: XDHYCD: 您 = "你；你们（含敬意）" (you, with respect), example "老师，～早！"; the polite question "您做什么工作？" is used to an adult in an HSK 2 sample. That elders use 你 to younger people is shown by the sample dialogues (e.g. "你的中文说得不错"), not stated as a rule.
rules.regional_note: 您 is much more frequent in northern (especially Beijing) speech; in the south many people use 你 even with older relatives. Using 您 to your partner's parents is still polite everywhere; if they make it clear that 你 is fine, follow their lead.

rules.rule: Answering a compliment with a modest deflection is still the norm, but the everyday forms have changed: in everyday speech 没有没有 / 哪有 are more common, or people accept with 谢谢 plus a modest note (谢谢，我还在学习). 您过奖了 and 还差得远呢 are polite and common, especially with elders; 哪里哪里 is understood everywhere but sounds bookish and old-fashioned to many younger speakers; 不敢当 is formal.
rules.why: The official 2002 list has a whole function “93. 谦虚” (modesty) with 哪里哪里 / 还差得远呢 / 马马虎虎吧 / 过奖了 / 不敢当; XDHYCD labels 过奖 and 哪里❺ as 谦辞 (humble words) for declining praise; the 2021 grammar standard still teaches 不敢当 (point 309). Current usage: teaching sites (That's Mandarin, DigMandarin, elon.io and others; WebSearch summaries) agree that 哪里哪里 now sounds bookish to many, that 没有没有 is the common colloquial reply, and that 谢谢 with a modest note is a natural middle way; native-written dialogue has 没有没有，您太客气了 and 谢谢，您过奖了 (RiSAWOZ).

rules.rule: 你多大了 is the everyday way to ask someone's age (you will hear it). To ask an older person, the everyday polite form is 您今年多大岁数了？ (XDHYCD 岁数, marked 〈口〉 colloquial: 他今年多大岁数了？); 高寿 is the respectful word for the very old (老大爷高寿啦？), and 贵庚 is a formal honorific for asking anyone's age.
rules.why: XDHYCD: 岁数 〈口〉 “人的年龄：……他今年多大～了？”; 高寿 ❷ “敬辞，用于问老人的年纪”; 贵庚 “敬辞，问人年龄”. 你多大了 is the everyday form (Tatoeba, HSK 1 sample).

rules.rule: Expect personal questions from the elders: your job (你做什么工作？), age (你多大了？), income (你一个月赚多少？) and, above all, marriage and children (你们什么时候结婚？ / 什么时候要孩子？). These questions are common at Chinese family gatherings — Chinese media publish features around Spring Festival on how to handle them. You do not have to answer precisely: a vague, friendly answer and a change of subject is the usual way out (还可以; 以后再说吧 said lightly), and your partner can field the hardest ones.
rules.why: Chinese media features on the questions relatives ask at Spring Festival (China Daily 2016; China News Service 2023/2024) and a Taiwanese analysis of the salary question; China News Service reports a China Youth Daily survey in which 59.2% of unmarried young people facing pressure to marry change the subject and 53.0% simply agree with whatever is said (all seen as WebSearch summaries). The 2025 HSK syllabus lists understanding family members' questions about work as a basic task.

scenes.title: Chinese New Year (春节 / 过年)
scenes.description: Greeting the partner's family over the Spring Festival: wishes for grandparents, children and colleagues, the New Year call (拜年), the reunion dinner and the Gala, zodiac small talk and festival taboos. The 2026 Year of the Horse began on 17 Feb 2026; the next Spring Festival is Sat 6 Feb 2027 (Year of the Goat/Sheep, New Year's Eve Fri 5 Feb 2027).

phrases.english: Happy New Year! (Spring Festival greeting)
phrases.usage: The default spoken greeting for the Spring Festival period, above all when you visit relatives (LTL: “Spring Festival only, especially when visiting relatives”); the new HSK syllabus gives it as the New Year greeting to know at level 2 (“过年说‘过年好’”). Say the person's family title first, then the greeting. Expect the same words back (过年好！) or 新年好！. Do not use it for 1 January — it belongs to the lunar New Year.
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: Used across mainland China. In Cantonese-speaking Guangdong 恭喜发财 is the everyday New Year greeting (LTL).

phrases.pinyin: Zhù nín zài xīn de yī nián shēntǐ jiànkāng!
phrases.literal: 祝 wish + 您 you (polite) + 在新的一年 in the new year + 身体 body + 健康 healthy
phrases.english: Wishing you good health in the new year!
phrases.usage: A health wish — the standard New Year wish for grandparents, the partner's parents and other elders (use 您; cf. zhihu: children wish elders 身体健康, CCTV: leaders wish elderly people 健康长寿). A shorter form is 祝你身体健康！ (YCT 4, CLEC) — with 您 for elders. In the official YCT sample the speaker adds 幸福快乐！ (answer C = 幸福) and gets the reply 谢谢你！也祝你新春快乐！
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 您 is used far more in northern (especially Beijing) speech; in many southern families 你 is normal even with elders in everyday talk. In a wish to an elder 您 is always polite and never wrong (forum discussions; anecdotal).

phrases.hanzi: 大妈，我们给您拜年来啦！
phrases.pinyin: Dàmā, wǒmen gěi nín bàinián lái la!
phrases.literal: 大妈 auntie + 我们 we + 给您 to you + 拜年 pay a New Year call + 来 come + 啦 (lively particle)
phrases.english: Auntie, we've come to wish you a Happy New Year!
phrases.usage: On the doorstep when you and your partner arrive at a relative's home during the New Year (拜年 = 向人祝贺新年, 现代汉语词典). Replace 大妈 with the person's family title (slot; ask your partner which title each relative gets). Shorter and more formal: 给您拜年了！ — a set New Year-call phrase used mainly on days 1–5 (see rule greeting-timing). Expect 过年好！ in return.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: Kinship titles vary by region and family (e.g. 外婆/外公 in most of the south vs 姥姥/姥爷 in the north for the mother's parents); use the titles your partner uses.

slots.meaning: the relative you are visiting, by family title (大妈 = the wife of the father's elder brother, i.e. 伯母; also a respectful word for any older woman — 现代汉语词典)

The dictionary example is 哥哥属马，弟弟属鸡; LTL gives 我属羊. Your own zodiac year comes round every 12 years (本命年).

rules.rule: Spring Festival dates: 2026 was the Year of the Horse (丙午马年): New Year's Eve (除夕) Mon 16 Feb 2026, Spring Festival (正月初一) Tue 17 Feb 2026, public holiday 15–23 Feb (9 days; make-up workdays Sat 14 Feb and Sat 28 Feb). Next: Year of the Goat/Sheep (丁未羊年) — New Year's Eve Fri 5 Feb 2027, Spring Festival Sat 6 Feb 2027, Lantern Festival Sat 20 Feb 2027. By law the Spring Festival holiday is 4 statutory days (除夕 to 初三), stretched by weekend swaps; the official 2027 arrangement had not been published on 2026-11-02 (the 2026 one was published in November 2025).
rules.why: Travel to the family has to be booked around these dates; greetings switch from “early” to “happy” to “late” New Year around them.

rules.rule: Timing of New Year wishes: from 小年 (23rd day of the 12th lunar month in the north, 24th in the south) until New Year's Eve you wish people an early New Year (拜个早年); from New Year's Day you say 过年好/新年好/新年快乐 and pay New Year calls (拜年) — closest family first, mainly days 1–5; after that, or when you first meet after the holiday, wishes become “late” (拜个晚年), and the New Year season in the broad sense lasts until the Lantern Festival (正月十五): 有心拜年，十五不晚. In 2027: 小年 Sat 30 Jan (north) / Sun 31 Jan (south); New Year's Eve Fri 5 Feb.
rules.why: Matching the wish to the date is part of sounding natural; a late wish is still welcome.
rules.regional_note: 小年 falls on 腊月二十三 in the north and 腊月二十四 in the south (陈连山 via Baidu Baike, People's Daily 2021); exact visiting customs vary by family and region.

rules.rule: Choose the wish for the person: elders (grandparents, the partner's parents) — use 您 and wish health and long life (身体健康, 健康长寿, 万事如意); school-age children and students — 学业进步 (or 学习进步, 快快长大 for small children); working adults and colleagues — 工作顺利, 步步高升, 恭喜发财; anyone — 新年快乐, 过年好, 万事如意, 心想事成 (friends, students). Several wishes are often chained: 身体健康、工作顺利、阖家幸福.
rules.why: Wishes are matched to the person's stage of life (LTL/search summary: students → 学业进步, anyone → 万事如意; CCTV: elderly people → 健康长寿).
rules.regional_note: 您 is used far more in northern (especially Beijing) speech; in many southern families 你 is normal even with elders in everyday talk. In a wish to an elder 您 is always polite and never wrong (forum discussions; anecdotal).

rules.rule: Firecrackers and fireworks are regulated city by city: under the State Council's 烟花爆竹安全管理条例 (art. 28) county-level and higher governments may restrict or ban them by time, place and type, and art. 30 bans them near cultural relics, stations and airports, etc. For the 2026 Spring Festival e.g. Nanjing kept bans in its central districts, Taiyuan banned them in all six urban districts, Zhengzhou banned them inside the 4th Ring Road but allowed them outside in set hours (e.g. New Year's Eve 07:00 to 01:00), and Yuncheng changed a full ban into restrictions; many places allow private use of small C/D-class products only. Check the local notice (通告) each year before setting any off; in April 2026 the State Council safety office started a one-year national crackdown on illegal fireworks.
rules.why: Setting off fireworks at a banned time or place is fined 100–500 yuan by the police (art. 42); the rules change from year to year and district to district.
rules.regional_note: Varies by city and even district; in 2026 outer districts were often more permissive than city centres (e.g. Zhengzhou outside the 4th Ring Road, Nanjing's central-district bans).

rules.rule: New Year's Eve is for the family reunion dinner (年夜饭/团圆饭) and the CCTV Gala, followed by staying up (守岁, 现代汉语词典: 在农历除夕晚上不睡觉，直到天亮). Dumplings are a must on New Year's Eve in northern China; southern tables have other symbolic foods — 年糕 (“higher year”; 现代汉语词典: 农历年的应时食品), fish and regional dishes, and in some southern areas sweet rice balls (汤圆) on the morning of New Year's Day. Fish is served for 年年有余 because 鱼 sounds like 余, and many families leave some of it uneaten — or keep the head and tail until New Year's Day — so that there is “surplus”; in Hubei a “look-at fish” (看鱼) is not eaten at all.
rules.why: Knowing the symbolism lets you comment on the dishes appropriately; do not assume a southern family will make dumplings.
rules.regional_note: Dumplings are a northern tradition; the partner's south/central family may serve 年糕, fish or regional dishes (e.g. CCTV 2023: families in Longyan, Fujian preparing 腊肉、笋干、手打牛肉丸 for the reunion dinner). Fish customs vary (not finished north of the Yangtze; head and tail kept for New Year's Day elsewhere; 看鱼 in Hubei) — watch the family before finishing the fish.

rules.rule: New Year visits follow an order: the 1st day is spent with the (husband's) family; in many regions married daughters return to their parents' home on the 2nd day (回娘家) with husband and children, bringing gifts in even numbers, and a son-in-law pays his respects to his wife's parents. The day differs locally (e.g. Qingdao on the 3rd, Dezhou on the 4th day).
rules.why: If you are married into the family, which day you visit whose parents is a real planning question — ask your partner what their family does.
rules.regional_note: Widespread on the 2nd day — e.g. Shandong, Hebei, Guangdong (Chaoshan and Hakka families), northern and central Shanxi, Henan (which also has a visit on the 16th of the 1st month) — but the day differs locally: Qingdao on the 3rd, Dezhou on the 4th, southern Shanxi mostly on the 3rd. Ask your partner's family.

rules.rule: Red envelopes go from older to younger and from married to unmarried: grandparents, parents, aunts and uncles give to children and to unmarried young adults (bosses also give to staff). Once you earn money you are expected to give to your own parents and grandparents, and once you marry you become a giver to the family's children.
rules.why: The envelope expresses the elder's care and good wishes (CCTV: 长辈对他们的关爱与期望); marriage moves you from the receiving to the giving side.

rules.rule: As an unmarried partner on a first New Year visit you are not expected to give the elders red envelopes (the custom runs elder → younger, married → unmarried); bring gifts for the parents instead. If the family has young children (the partner's younger siblings, nieces, nephews), many visitors give each child an envelope — the same amount for each, a round even sum (one zhihu article: 50–200 yuan is common for minors); some also give close grandparents 100–500 yuan with a written wish. Be ready to receive one yourself: parents often give a partner they meet for the first time a red envelope (见面礼). Ask your partner what the family and province expect before you go.
rules.why: Customs differ by province and family, and both giving too little and giving where it is not expected can embarrass people.
rules.regional_note: Amounts differ widely: Guangdong is modest (利是 of 5–50 yuan), Zhejiang, Fujian, Jiangsu and Shanghai are among the most generous (see rule amounts).

rules.rule: Avoid amounts containing 4 (四 sì sounds like 死 sǐ, death) and 250 (二百五 means “idiot”); prefer even sums and 6s and 8s (e.g. 200, 600, 666, 800, 888); give children of the same family the same amount. Typical sums vary enormously: Guangdong 利是 are often 5–10 yuan (50 already counts as generous), while 2026 media figures put ordinary relatives' children at about 200–500 yuan and close relatives at 666–2,000 in Zhejiang or Shanghai, and 500–1,000 for ordinary relatives in parts of Fujian; the north starts around 100. The often-shared “national red-envelope map” is 2018 data.
rules.why: Numbers carry meaning (homophones), and the expected amount depends on region, closeness and income.
rules.regional_note: Guangdong: small and widespread; Zhejiang/Fujian/Jiangsu/Shanghai: large; ask the partner for the family's usual figure.
